name: Tomas Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel; we have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential, so what does your shift look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am a senior operator at a glass bottle plant, where hot glass drops into moulds on the forming line. My two-year technical diploma helps me set the section timing, and I check the first bottle for a thin wall. The pay is above the usual operator rate and the furnace makes you respect every safety barrier.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What fills the rest of your week, and do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Hanna and I are repairing a small cottage, with a manageable loan and over six months of expenses saved. There are plenty of other plants nearby, though I would compare actual pay before moving. I use AI now and then to tidy a repair list, but I adopt a new control only after I have seen it work on a real section.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the hot-end crew the little AI report is useful for planning maintenance, but a bottle with a thin shoulder still goes in the reject bin. The furnace does not care how neat the report looks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bottle orders are steady and I earn the senior rate for keeping the forming sections in tune. My partner Hanna and I have more than six months saved, and there are several other plants nearby if this one slows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep setting gob timing and checking the first bottles after each mould change. In the first year of the plateau I would use AI now and then to tidy a repair list for our cottage, then pay an extra amount from new wages against its small loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. The repair list can be faster, and the glass still needs watching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you spot a thin shoulder?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I hold the first bottle against the lamp and see where the glass stretches near the neck. Then I check the wall gauge before accepting the batch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the loan payment new money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, the usual payment is already in our budget. Hanna and I would add a little from each new senior-rate pay packet to bring the balance down.

say: I would tell the **hot-end crew** a neat report cannot release a thin-walled bottle.
I would keep **AI repair lists** as a small household convenience.
think: Steady **bottle orders** and the senior rate make my current work secure.
Our **savings** and nearby plants give Hanna and me room to choose.
do: Set **gob timing** and inspect the first bottles after mould changes.
Pay **extra cottage loan** principal from new senior-rate wages.
feel: **Calm**, because the work and household finances look steady.
S0.quote: The furnace does not care how neat the report looks.
fieldNote: Tomas uses AI **now and then** for a household list, while physical bottle checks remain his work.
The extra **loan payment** comes from new wages, building the cushion rather than moving existing savings.

steps.text: Keep forming bottles and checking first pieces after mould changes
Pay extra cottage loan principal from new senior-rate wages

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the plant that quicker furnace scheduling is fine after it has survived a full week on one section. I would ask the setter to show me every fault the new control missed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My senior setting role should remain useful, but fewer changeovers might mean less overtime. Hanna’s pharmacy wage looks steady, yet a recurring reduction in mine would change our cottage repair budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my usual forming shift and record the overtime on the next four rosters. If the plant offers a paid place to learn the new temperature control after a guarded trial, I would practise on one section; if overtime falls twice, we would delay the cottage windows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a real pay cut, though interested once the control proves itself. I have saved enough to avoid rushing into a bad decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would prove the control works?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It must hold bottle wall thickness through a whole week of mould changes, with the operator able to stop a bad run. A temperature-control chart from one afternoon cannot prove glass bottle quality through a week of mould changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn it before the trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I use AI occasionally at home, but a furnace control is different and needs paid instruction on a guarded section. I want the old setter beside me.

say: I would ask for a **full-week trial** before trusting new furnace scheduling.
I would keep the **operator stop** available during every new control test.
think: My **overtime** may fall if changeovers get faster.
Hanna’s **pharmacy wage** and our savings help, though cottage repairs would wait.
do: Learn the **temperature control** only if offered paid guarded practice after a proven trial.
Delay **cottage windows** after two reduced overtime rosters.
feel: **Anxious** about recurring overtime loss, with room to respond.
S1.quote: A temperature-control chart from one afternoon cannot prove glass bottle quality through a week of mould changes.
fieldNote: His steady style asks for **production evidence** across one full week before new control practice.
Learning is conditional on **paid guarded instruction**, while a two-roster pay loss triggers a repair delay.

steps.text: Learn temperature control if offered paid guarded practice after proven trial
Delay cottage windows after two reduced overtime rosters

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew thinking AI by 2028 could plan bottle runs, when I am twenty nine. Capable hands-on robots around 2031, when I am thirty two, are the part that could take forming sections away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hot end may keep a setter for a while, but I could lose senior shifts if robot tending becomes reliable. Our savings and Hanna’s wage cover time to search, not the whole working life I have ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check the plant’s staffing plan and keep my paid forming work while it remains safe. If two rosters cut my hours, I would apply for a posted nearby glass-plant role only at a comparable base wage and with written safe furnace access; I would stop the new window order meanwhile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my own pay, but not helpless. The machine has taught me to wait for a measurement before I change the setting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you operate a capable robot immediately?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for a supervised paid trial on one guarded section and watch the first bottles. I would not operate its controls until a paid place is offered and a safety lead signs the isolation checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if another plant offers lower pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the wage against our cottage loan and ordinary bills with Hanna. I would not leave a paid shift for a lower rate just because a job title says robot.

say: I would distinguish **2028 planning AI** from 2031 hands-on bottle robots.
I would ask for a **paid guarded trial** before robot controls reach my section.
think: My **senior shifts** could shrink when robots tend forming sections.
Savings and **Hanna’s wage** buy time, not a replacement lifetime income.
do: Keep **paid forming work** while the furnace remains safely staffed.
Apply after **two cut rosters** to a posted comparable-pay local role with written safe access.
Stop the **window order** while pay is uncertain.
feel: **Anxious** about senior shift loss, with savings and job options.
S2.quote: I would not leave a paid shift for a lower rate just because a job title says robot.
fieldNote: He separates a **robot trial request** from any actual hands-on practice.
His fallback has a **two-roster trigger** and requires a real local posting, comparable base pay and safe access.

steps.text: Keep paid forming work while safely staffed
Apply after two cut rosters for posted comparable-pay safe local role
Pause cottage window order while pay is uncertain

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew five years gives us time to watch real forming trials. Thinking AI arrives in 2031 when I am thirty two, and capable hands-on robots about 2034 when I am thirty five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can keep earning on the hot end during the warning, but that does not settle what work pays after 2034. A plant maintenance role would fit my diploma only with practical instruction and a posted vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would ask the plant about a fully funded maintenance course with paid workshop days and a place on a stopped furnace section. If it is offered and a local maintenance job at comparable base pay is posted, I would enrol; after qualifying, I would apply for that role only if the safe access duties are written, while keeping my current shift until then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with a plan I can test instead of guessing. I will not sign up for unpaid study because a robot date is on a card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the course have to teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would diagnose a faulty section drive with the furnace isolated and a qualified fitter watching. The course must cover actual repair work, not only a video of buttons.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could the course guarantee you a job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. A posted local vacancy and comparable pay are separate questions after qualification. I would stay on the hot end if those conditions fail.

I would separate **2031 planning AI** from later hands-on work.
think: Current **hot-end wages** help me prepare, but the post-2034 role is uncertain.
A **maintenance course** needs practical instruction and a real paid opening.
do: Request a **funded paid-time course** with a stopped-section workshop place.
Enrol only if **offered** that course and a posted comparable-pay local maintenance job.

feel: **Uneasy**, with real course and job conditions to check.
S3.quote: I will not sign up for unpaid study because a robot date is on a card.
fieldNote: His course enquiry becomes **conditional enrolment** only after an offered paid practical place and posted fair-wage job.
The later **job application** depends on qualification and written safe access, while current wages continue.

steps.text: Enrol in funded paid-time maintenance course if workshop place and posted comparable-pay job exist
Apply after qualifying for posted comparable-pay local role with safe access
Keep current hot-end shift until suitable role opens

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say ten years before thinking AI in 2036 is long enough to learn from real machines. Capable hands-on robots around 2039 are thirteen years from now, so the hot end still needs safe operators for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be thirty seven when thinking AI arrives and forty when capable robots reach the forming work. The cottage loan may be gone by then, but Hanna and I will still need income, and a good decade does not promise a job afterward.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep running forming shifts and pay extra cottage loan principal from new wages. In the first year after 2036 I would inspect actual rosters and nearby postings; if my current shift remains paid and safe I would stay, but after sustained cuts I would apply only to a posted comparable-pay role with written furnace safety duties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the long end of the story, but calm enough to keep a measured plan. I have time to see what works instead of betting the cottage on a forecast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a robot for the plant now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That is the owner’s decision. A robot forecast is not a glass-plant purchasing case. I would ask for measured bottle quality and guarded trials before anyone changes the line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change jobs before 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two reduced rosters and a posted local opening at comparable pay with safe access. If the present plant keeps paying a good rate, I would rather continue the work I know.

say: I would say **2036 thinking AI** comes before 2039 forming robots.
I would ask for **measured bottle quality** before any machine purchase.
think: At **forty**, I still need income even if the cottage loan is gone.
The long **wage runway** gives time without promising a job after robots.
do: Keep **forming shifts** now and pay extra loan principal from new wages.
Check **post-2036 rosters** and apply after sustained cuts only to posted comparable-pay safe local roles.
feel: **Uneasy** about later wages, with time for a measured plan.
S4.quote: A robot forecast is not a glass-plant purchasing case.
fieldNote: Tomas distinguishes the **ten-year thinking date** from a thirteen-year wait for capable forming robots.
His post-2036 work and job application retain **material conditions** on paid shifts, actual postings, comparable pay and furnace safety.

steps.text: Keep current forming shifts while safely paid

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because robots might reduce my senior forming hours around 2031, early in a long working life. Paid guarded trials, a funded practical course and posted local jobs at comparable pay would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who stops a forming section when the first bottle has a thin shoulder. A good bottle cannot be argued into shape by a tidy report.

headlineQuote: A good bottle cannot be argued into shape by a tidy report.
portrait: **Tomas**, 27, runs hot-end forming machines at a glass bottle plant with a two-year technical diploma.
His **higher pay**, partner, strong savings and many nearby plants give him a cushion, though he compares actual wages.
He uses AI **occasionally** and adopts controls after measured production and guarded practice prove them.
Fast robots threaten **senior shifts**; more warning allows a funded practical maintenance route if a real job opens.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could lead to reduced forming shifts around 2031, early in Tomas’s working life.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid guarded trials**, funded practical training and posted comparable-pay local work would help him choose.
